Messages.Author: Jozxyqk
Messages.Body:
---
Politics works the same way in Anarchs as it always has, except that the
rule against replacing cards during a referendum has been dropped. Cards
are replaced during a referendum as normal. Note that each Methuselah is
still limited to using no more than one Political Card to gain a vote in
each referendum.
---

I like this.
I never understood the purpose of the "can't replace cards during a
referendum" rule in the first place.

This means no more answering the "can I play a voter cap after I've
replaced my cards post-referendum" question.

It also means that defensive voting has gotten a little stronger.
You can play Forced Awakenings during the referendum to see if you
can draw into your Delaying Tactics when things are looking grim. :)

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
>I like this.
>I never understood the purpose of the "can't replace cards during a
>referendum" rule in the first place.

My initial reaction towards this change was actually negative, if only because
I prefer maintaining the status quo.

I can understand why this was done however. I think the "no replacing" rule was
originally introduced primarily to limit "vote pushing" back when there wasn't
a limit to how many PA's you could ditch. I suppose now that there has been a
limit (1 per Methusaleh) for quite some time, the rule is a bit obsolete.

Thus I do agree that this change does streamline things a bit more by tossing a
special exception case out the window. Some of us will still remember "the old
days" however when you couldn't replace...

Halcyan 2

It actually goes back as far as Jyhad, it wasn't really "introduced".

http://www.crystalkeep.com/tcg/vtes/rules/jyhad-rules.txt

Note that no cards played during a vote are
replaced until after the vote.

That meant that no more than 7 PAs (excluding Elder Library etc.) could
be thrown down during a vote.

I'm very uncertain of whether or not real power politics was ever tried
by Garfield and friends during testing, though. It seems to have been a
nice curve ball and third leg of the game, but it's hard to tell if it
was ever a big thing.

Actually in an interview in the Jyhad book Garfield
says that a playtesting goal was balancing the
3 main deck types; bleed, combat monster, and
political.

The vote pushing business may or may not have
been playtested. The written rules in Jyhad actually
spelled out the current system (indicating playtesting,
since it's a weird rule out of context) but the rules
team quickly allowed unlimited (well, hand-limited)
vote pushing. The original rules team was out to
lunch an awful lot, though.

this text document is not actually what's written in the jyhad
rulebook. i have a hard copy right here in my sweaty little hand, and
this is what it says:

"A political card always provides one vote for the Methuselah playing
it. This card is immediately replaced after being played. Additional
political cards can also be used by any of the other Methuselahs for
votes. The actual effects of these cards are ignored. Cards used in
this way are discarded to the ash heap and not replaced until the
voting is finished."

which to my mind means that vote pushing for the acting methuselah
was, in fact, not allowed in jyhad origionally. The first two
sentances seem to refer to the political action card used to call the
referendum, and the other parts seem to only refer to the non-acting
methuselahs. only those non-acting methuselahs are not allowed to
replace political action cards. but they are allowed to replace other
cards played during a referendum.

i guess the state the game got into later on was a result of bungled
clarifications/rulings on the situation.

it's all quite interesting, really.

salem.
